cues.text: Section five: disaster recovery and operational metrics.
Let's begin with two ideas that sound similar but are not the same.
Business continuity is about keeping critical business processes operating.
Disaster recovery is narrower: it is about restoring IT systems after a disruption.
So business continuity asks, how does the organisation keep doing its essential work?
Disaster recovery asks, how do we get the technology back?
Now we need two measures that define how good a recovery must be.
The first is RTO, which stands for Recovery Time Objective.
This is the target maximum time allowed to restore service.
The second is RPO, which stands for Recovery Point Objective.
This is the tolerable amount of data loss, measured in time.
Let's work through the example from the source.
Suppose the RPO is fifteen minutes, and a failure happens at ten o'clock.
That means you aim to recover data at least through nine forty-five, because fifteen minutes before ten is nine forty-five.
Anything written between nine forty-five and the failure is the loss you have agreed to tolerate.
Now suppose the RTO is one hour.
With the failure at ten o'clock, you must restore service by eleven o'clock.
Notice the difference: RPO looks backwards, at how much data you can afford to lose.
RTO looks forwards, at how long you can afford to be down.
A warning about replication.
Replication copies data to another location, which is useful, but it can also copy corruption.
If bad data or damaged records are written on the primary system, replication may faithfully copy them to the secondary one as well.
That is why backups and restore tests remain necessary.
A backup you have never tested restoring is only a hope, not a plan.
Next, the types of alternate recovery site.
A hot site is ready quickly, but it is costly.
A warm site is partially prepared, so it sits in the middle.
A cold site requires setup before it can be used, so it is cheaper but slower.
You can see the trade-off: the faster you need to recover, the more you generally pay.
Two more terms, and they are a pair.
Failover means moving to alternate resources when the primary fails.
Failback means restoring operations to the primary safely once it is available again.
Failback is not simply flipping back; the word safely matters.
Finally, good recovery needs documentation.
Document the incident roles, so people know who does what.
Document communications, so stakeholders are informed.
Document exercises, so the plan is practised rather than only written.
And document recovery verification, so you can confirm that systems and data are genuinely restored.
Now let's move to operational metrics, starting with the DORA delivery metrics.
These commonly include four measures.
First, deployment frequency, which is how often you deploy.
Second, change lead time, which runs from commit to production.
Third, change failure rate.
Fourth, failed deployment recovery time, which is how long it takes to recover when a deployment fails.
The source adds a qualification: the definitions, and any additional measures that have evolved over time, vary.
So treat these as common rather than fixed.
Be careful not to conflate change lead time with business request lead time.
Change lead time starts at the commit and ends in production.
Business request lead time concerns the request itself, and is a different thing.
Change failure rate has a formula.
It equals failed deployments, divided by total deployments, multiplied by one hundred percent.
For example, three failures out of thirty deployments is three divided by thirty, which is zero point one, and times one hundred percent gives ten percent.
The wider lesson is to balance speed and stability: delivering fast is not enough if many changes fail, and being stable is not enough if delivery is very slow.
The last topic is FinOps, which the source labels a supplementary CA concept.
It is about managing cloud cost.
The practices listed are these: identify orphaned storage; rightsize idle resources; review unused commitments and discount plans; tag costs; and monitor unit economics.
Two cautions apply.
Deleting unattached disks requires retention, backup and owner checks first.
Just because a disk is unattached does not mean it is safe to delete.
And existing reserved commitments need separate optimisation, meaning they are not solved by simply deleting resources.
